title: The Bible and the Ancient Near East
lead: Israel lived among older civilizations, in Mesopotamia, Egypt and Canaan, whose texts sometimes parallel the Bible closely. This page gathers the main parallels, with an honest verdict on each: shared tradition, borrowing, protest, or mere likeness. This page covers the texts of the ancient Near East and their parallels anywhere in the Bible; for later or non-Near-Eastern myths of the end of the world, see Other Traditions.

sections.b:
Enuma Elish (Babylonian creation epic, known form about 1100 BC): Marduk defeats the sea goddess Tiamat and makes the world from her body. Shared themes: watery beginning, a sky dividing waters, humans made last. Verdict: Genesis 1 shares a world of ideas but tells a different story, with no battle and no rival gods; many read it as a quiet protest.

Atrahasis (Old Babylonian; the oldest dated copy was written about 1630 BC, and the poem is older): gods make humans from clay and divine blood to do their work, then send a flood when humans are too noisy; Atrahasis builds a boat. It runs from creation to flood like Genesis 1–9. Verdict: a real shared outline, very different gods.

Gilgamesh, Tablet XI: Utnapishtim's flood, with a boat, birds and a sacrifice the gods smell. Verdict: the closest parallel in the Bible's world. Nearly all scholars agree that the two share a tradition; most critical scholars think Genesis depends on it, directly or indirectly; many conservatives think both descend from a common memory.

The Sumerian King List (about 1800 BC): long-lived kings before a flood. Verdict: a similar shape to Genesis 5, on a vastly larger scale.

sections.b: The laws of Hammurabi of Babylon (about 1750 BC) and older codes from Ur and Eshnunna use the same "if a man..." form as the laws of Exodus 21–23, and some cases are close: the goring ox (Exodus 21:28–32) and the "eye for eye" principle (Exodus 21:23–25). Verdict: shared legal culture; the Bible differs in grounding law in God's covenant and in protecting slaves and foreigners more. Hittite treaties of the 1300s BC and Assyrian treaties of the 600s BC share the shape of Deuteronomy (history, stipulations, witnesses, blessings and curses). Scholars debate which treaty form Deuteronomy follows, which bears on its date.

The tablets of Ugarit on the Syrian coast (1300s–1200s BC) tell how Baal the storm god defeated Yamm, the sea, and the seven-headed serpent Litan, and was enthroned. The Bible borrows the language and turns it to the LORD: he crushes the heads of Leviathan (Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 27:1), rules the flood (Psalm 29:3–10), and rides the clouds (Psalm 68:4). Revelation's seven-headed dragon (Revelation 12:3) draws on the same imagery. Verdict: clear borrowing of poetic images, used to claim for Israel's God what Canaan said of Baal.

sections.b: The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope (about 1100 BC) has thirty chapters of advice, and Proverbs 22:17–24:22 follows it closely in places, even speaking of "thirty sayings" (Proverbs 22:20). Verdict: most scholars, conservative and critical, accept that Proverbs here adapts Amenemope.

common: Genesis is simply a copy of Babylonian myths.
The parallels were unknown until skeptics invented them.
uncommon: The Babylonian flood stories may themselves combine older Sumerian traditions, such as the story of Ziusudra.
Genesis may have been shaped partly in conversation with Babylon during the exile.
